subject: technology
topic: Following GPS may wear down your own sense of direction
angle: While heavy GPS use is linked to a decline in spatial memory and reduced brain connectivity, it does not appear to directly impact actual navigational abilities in experimental settings.
title: The Erosion of Internal Maps

hooks.text: Where do you go when your phone dies?
You can navigate perfectly, yet your brain is losing its map.
You are outsourcing your spatial memory to a satellite.
A blue line on a glass screen.
GPS use is linked to memory decline.

reveal.headline: Your brain is losing its internal map.
reveal.body: Heavy GPS use is linked to a steeper decline in hippocampal-dependent spatial memory and reduced brain connectivity.

explain.headline: The evidence is mixed.
explain.body: Studies show a correlation between high GPS usage and poorer spatial memory. However, experiments show that using GPS navigation in AR glasses does not change actual navigational abilities.

matters.headline: The map is no longer in your head.
matters.body: That may be why you feel lost without your phone. The hippocampus organizes your experiences as a relational memory. By outsourcing your route, you may be thinning the structure of your own mental landscape.

example.headline: The familiar turn.
example.body: You drive to a friend's house. You see the turn ahead, but you do not recognize the street name or the landmarks. You wait for the blue line to tell you when to move.

question.headline: Where would you go if your phone died?

stat.label: change in hippocampal-dependent spatial memory over three years

claims.text: Using GPS navigation in AR glasses for three months does not change navigational abilities.
claims.quote: Importantly, no effect of intervention on navigational abilities was observed.

claims.text: Greater GPS use over a three-year period was linked to a steeper decline in hippocampal-dependent spatial memory.
claims.quote: we observed an important effect of GPS use over time, whereby greater GPS use since initial testing was associated with a steeper decline in hippocampal-dependent spatial memory.

claims.text: Using GPS navigation in AR glasses for three months reduces the functional coupling between the hippocampus and associated brain regions.
claims.quote: the experimental group showed FC decrease after three months of using GPS navigation implemented in AR glasses in contrast to FC increase in the control group without such intervention.

claims.text: People with more lifetime GPS experience are linked to worse spatial memory when they have to navigate without GPS.
claims.quote: We first present cross-sectional results that show that people with greater lifetime GPS experience have worse spatial memory during self-guided navigation, i. e. when they are required to navigate without GPS.

claims.text: The hippocampus is not dedicated solely to spatial cognition and navigation, but organizes experiences in memory, where spatial mapping is a metaphor for relational memory organization.
claims.quote: These observations suggest that the hippocampal system is not dedicated to spatial cognition and navigation, but organizes experiences in memory, for which spatial mapping and navigation are both a metaphor for and a prominent application of relational memory organization.

verdict: The evidence shows a correlation between high GPS usage and poorer spatial memory and reduced hippocampal connectivity, but it does not prove that GPS use causes a loss of navigation skills.
caveat: The longitudinal study showing memory decline had a small sample size, and the experiment showing no change in navigational abilities may have limitations regarding the mechanism of change.
caption:
Your phone is drawing the map, but your brain is losing the territory.

Research shows a correlation between high GPS usage and poorer spatial memory and reduced hippocampal connectivity. However, a small study suggests that navigational abilities in experimental settings may remain unchanged.
